conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS). This is a short, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past seven days. Everything you share stays confidential, and my goal is simply to support you and your baby in these early weeks. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong answers.

Shall we begin?

Over the last seven days, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has it felt hard to feel excited about anything?

Honestly, it’s been pretty hard to feel excited. I used to look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or texting a friend—but right now they just feel… flat. Even when my mom offers to watch the baby so I can nap or shower, I don’t get that “yes, finally!” feeling I thought I would. I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t really there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like yesterday when my husband made a silly face and the baby startled himself with his own hiccup—but it takes a lot more effort than it used to. Most of the time I feel like I’m faking it so people won’t worry.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. Even when I know I “should” feel excited—like when my sister said she’d bring dinner or when I planned a short walk—I mostly feel… nothing. I still say yes and go through the motions, but the happy anticipation just isn’t there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I didn’t hold him long enough, or I’m just not cut out for this. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap, and I sat there crying, convinced it was my fault for not reading his cues properly. Even when people tell me babies just cry, I still feel like I’m failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. My mind keeps spinning with “what-ifs”—what if he stops breathing when I’m in the shower, what if the formula’s too hot, what if I fall asleep while feeding him and drop him? There’s no real reason; he’s healthy and the doctor says he’s doing great. But the worry just sits in my chest anyway, and I can’t shake it, even when I tell myself it’s irrational.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing and I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby monitor or go peek in the bassinet even if I just left him sleeping. There’s no real trigger; it just hits out of nowhere and then fades after a few minutes, but it leaves me feeling on edge for the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the dishes piling up, or I’ll hear my phone buzz with messages I haven’t answered, and suddenly it’s like everything’s closing in. I usually manage to get the essentials done, but it’s exhausting and I end up crying in the kitchen more often than I care to admit.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—replay­ing every little thing I might have done wrong, worrying about the next feed, listening for every squeak from the bassinet. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again. I probably get three or four broken hours, and by morning I feel just as tired as when I went to bed.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest, like I’m already behind before I even open my eyes. Little things that used to feel neutral—like the morning light or my favorite mug—just make me want to cry. I keep telling myself it’s hormones or sleep deprivation, but the sadness lingers no matter what I do.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three, maybe four times this week. Yesterday it was because I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter—totally fixable, but I just sat on the kitchen floor and sobbed. Most times there’s no big trigger; the tears kind of build up and spill over, and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom to my baby.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has quietly slipped away-morning coffee, a friend's text, even offers of help feel flat and distant. You describe constant worry, sudden waves of panic, and a daily heaviness that makes even small tasks feel overwhelming. Despite putting on a brave face, you're exhausted, tearful, and blaming yourself whenever your baby fusses; yet you emphatically deny any wish to harm yourself and simply long to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports reduced ability to laugh and describes needing to fake enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports "the happy anticipation just isn't there anymore" and "feel… nothing," indicating an almost complete loss of enjoyment which aligns with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for routine infant behaviors, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries occurring "pretty much all the time" with physical tension and inability to control them, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes that occur repeatedly and intrusively, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and tears but still managing essentials, matching "sometimes not coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep, fragmented sleep, and waking unrested—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with tearfulness and emotional heaviness matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week with difficulty stopping, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS ≥14 strongly suggests <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse daily sadness, loss of interest, disproportionate self-blame, psychomotor agitation with panic surges, middle insomnia, and frequent crying-meeting five <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for at least two weeks. Combined with constant <sym>anxiety</sym> and functional impairment, urgent evaluation is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within one week
2. Discuss therapy options-<med>CBT</med> or interpersonal therapy specialized for postpartum mood
3. Screen for <med>thyroid dysfunction</med> and anemia to rule out medical contributors
4. Enlist partner or family for overnight infant care to allow 4-5 hour sleep blocks
5. Limit daily goals to one priority; accept help with chores and meals
6. Arrange follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
7. Call 988 (or local crisis line) immediately if mood worsens or self-harm thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) – patient self-report, 2–3 wks postpartum.

Symptoms endorsed (severity: mild–moderate):  
- Persistent low mood, sadness, tearfulness (daily)  
- Marked anhedonia; absence of anticipatory pleasure  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-ifs,” physical tension  
- Panic-like surges (no discrete trigger)  
- Overwhelm, feeling “treading water,” situational crying spells  
- Initial & middle insomnia related to rumination and hyper-vigilance about infant safety  

Positive findings for postpartum depression & anxiety screening:  
- EPDS items 1, 2, 8, 9 indicate probable depressive symptoms  
- Items 4, 5, 6 suggest clinically significant anxiety  
- Item 10 (self-harm ideation): negative – no safety concern at present  

Risk factors noted:  
- Sleep deprivation compounding mood lability  
- High self-expectations / perfectionism  
- Absence of suicidal ideation; nevertheless requires monitoring

Summary:  
Patient reports multiple depressive and anxious symptoms exceeding “baby blues” expectations, with functional impact on sleep, coping, and emotional bonding. No self-harm reported. Recommend further evaluation (diagnostic interview, psychosocial supports, possible treatment referral) and routine safety reassessment.
